21-038.r: When Raja Wodeyar founded Mysore (1612 A.D.), Vijayanagara ruler → Venkata II (Aravidu, capital Chandragiri); Aravidu began when Tirumala ousted Sadasiva (1570 AD).

21-039.r: Chief feature of Vijayanagara finance → land revenue, fixed after measuring and grading land; tax 'Shist' (Rai Rekha); revenue department 'Athavane'.

21-040.r: Both correct: Krishna Deva's land tax varied with land quality (wet, dry, orchards, woods); private workshop owners paid an industry tax.

21-041.r: Ruins of the old Vijayanagara capital → Hampi (central Karnataka); Virupaksha temple; UNESCO World Heritage Site.

21-043.r: Vijayanagara capital Hampi → on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra (now Vijayanagara district, Karnataka).

21-044.r: Vijayanagara ruler who sent an embassy to the Chinese emperor → Bukka I (1356-77 AD), in 1374 AD.

21-045.r: Telugu poet Srinath (1365-1441 AD) → court of Deva Raya II; also served Reddy ruler Pedakomati Vema of Kondavidu.
21-045.c: Book notes CGPSC deleted this question in its revised answer key.

21-046.r: Kalyana Mandapas (halls for divine weddings) → notable feature of Vijayanagara temples.
21-046.t: Don't pick Chalukya, Chandela or Rashtrakuta; Kalyana Mandapa is a Vijayanagara hallmark.

21-047.r: Vijaya Vitthala temple with 56 musical pillars → Hampi; built by Krishnadeva Raya (1509-29 AD), continued under Achyutaraya.

21-048.r: Dance tradition first developed under Vijayanagara → Yakshagana, folk dance of coastal Karnataka on mythological stories.

22-001.r: Barani did not call the Sultanate truly Islamic because the majority of the population did not follow Islam.

22-002.r: Most Sultans and amirs of the Sultanate period → Turkish; amirs grew powerful when the Sultan was weak or a child.

22-003.r: Only 1 correct: Amil collected revenue in a Pargana. Wrong: Iqta was not indigenous; Mir Bakshi was a Mughal office, not Khalji.

22-004.r: Not true of Iqta: revenue went straight to the Sultan. Muqti kept it for administration and troops; Iqta introduced by Iltutmish; Siyasatnama a source.

22-005.r: A true: Sultanate land = Khalisa and Jagirs (Iqta). R false: Khalisa was under direct state control; a Jagir was a revenue assignment, not state-held land.
22-005.t: Khalisa = crown land; Jagir/Iqta = assigned land. Don't swap them.

22-006.r: Ascending size: Pargana (Shiqdar) < Sarkar (Faujdar) < Suba (Subedar); villages lay under the Pargana.
22-006.h: P-S-S: Pargana → Sarkar → Suba, small to big.

22-007.r: Diwan-i-Arz (military department) → Balban (1266-1286 A.D.), separated from Diwan-i-Wizarat (finance).

22-008.r: Wrong pair: Diwan-i-Riyasat–Balban; it was Alauddin's market-control department. Correct: Mustakhraj–Alauddin; Amir-i-Kohi–Muhammad bin Tughluq; Khairat–Firuz Tughluq.

22-009.r: Correct: Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves) → Firuz Shah Tughluq. Mustakhraj → Alauddin Khalji; Amir-i-Kohi → Muhammad bin Tughluq; Arz → Balban.

22-010.r: Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi → agriculture department of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, giving direct aid to farmers to bring more land under cultivation.

22-012.r: Diwan-i-Arz → military; Diwan-i-Risalat → religious (and foreign) matters; Diwan-i-Insha → state correspondence; Diwan-i-Wizarat → finance.

22-014.r: Heyday of the Wizarat → Tughluq era; Wazir (prime minister) headed Diwan-i-Wizarat (finance); first Wazir in India: Abbas Fazal-bin-Ahmad under Mahmud Ghaznavi.

22-015.r: Medieval government → a fusion of Perso-Arabic, Turko-Mongol (Central Asian) and Indian elements.

22-016.r: Taxes on land produce → Kharaj, Ushr, Muktai; Khums is one-fifth of war booty, not a land tax.

22-017.r: Iqta system introduced in the Delhi Sultanate → Iltutmish; Iqta = land given to officers in lieu of salary (Caliphate practice from the 9th century).

22-018.r: Iqta → land revenue (assignment); Mahrousa → protected town; Khalisa → land under state administration; Shiq → a portion of land.

22-019.r: Muqaddam or Chaudhari → village headman, the highest revenue authority in the village.

22-021.r: Supreme rural land-revenue official in the Sultanate → Chaudhary (village headman), used to collect revenue as Rais' influence was cut.

22-022.r: 'Sharb' (Haqq-i-Sharb) → irrigation tax, 10% of yield, levied by Firuz Tughluq; he kept four Quranic taxes (Kharaj, Jizya, Khums, Zakat) and abolished 21 others.

22-023.r: Zawabits → state laws (Sultan's own regulations) in the Sultanate period.

22-024.r: Hadis (Hadith) → source of Islamic law: reports of Prophet Muhammad's sayings, customs and deeds.

22-026.r: Fawazil → excess (surplus) revenue paid by Iqtadars to the exchequer.

22-027.r: Two main Sultanate coins → Tanka (silver) and Jital (copper), both started by Iltutmish.
22-027.t: Dam and Rupiya are later coins (Akbar, Sher Shah), not the Sultanate's main pair.

22-030.r: Tanka and Shashgani → silver; Jital → copper; regular currency first issued by Iltutmish; Tanka : Jital = 1:48.

22-031.r: Last Baghdad Caliph Al-Mustasim's name first on coins of → Alauddin Masud Shah (1242-1246 A.D.); Iltutmish's coins carried Caliph Mustansir's name.

23-001.r: Paper in India → used from about 7th-8th century CE; paper documents by 11th century; royal use 12-13th century; so none of the given centuries.
23-001.c: Book's answer (e) differs from BPSC's key, which gave (a) 12th century CE.

23-002.r: Alai Darwaza → Alauddin Khalji; domed red sandstone gateway with white marble, completed 1311 AD; early Indo-Islamic building.

23-003.r: Horse-shoe arch first used → Alai Darwaza, built by Alauddin Khalji.
23-003.t: Don't confuse: first true arch = Balban's tomb; horse-shoe arch = Alai Darwaza.

23-004.r: No role in Qutub Minar → Alauddin Khalji. Aybak built the base, Iltutmish completed it, Firuz Shah Tughluq restored the fourth and added the fifth storey.

23-006.r: Only 2 correct: Chand Minar (fifteenth century) is 210 ft, four storeys. Qutub Minar (thirteenth century, five storeys) is 238 ft (72.5 m), not 180 ft.

23-007.r: India's first tomb in Indo-Islamic style (per book) → Balban's tomb, Mehrauli, New Delhi; built 1287 AD in rubble masonry.

23-008.r: First true arch in a Sultanate monument → Tomb of Balban, Mehrauli, New Delhi.
23-008.h: Balban = first 'B'ow (true arch); Alai Darwaza = horse-shoe arch.

23-009.r: Order: Qutub Minar (Aybak, Iltutmish) → Tughluqabad fort (Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, 1320-1325) → Lodi Garden (Lodis, 1451-1526) → Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar).

23-010.r: Sultan Garhi → Iltutmish; Red Palace → Balban; Jamat Khana Masjid (Nizamuddin dargah) → Khizr Khan, Alauddin's son; Adhai Din ka Jhopra → Qutbuddin Aybak.
23-010.c: No exact code: the book says Khizr Khan, Alauddin Khalji's son, built Jamat Khana Masjid. Only code (c) 3 4 1 2 gets the other three pairs right, linking it to Alauddin.

23-011.r: Wrong pair: Hindola Mahal–Hoshang Shah; built by Ghiyas-ud-din Khalji (also Jahaz Mahal). Correct: Lal Mahal–Balban; Lal Darwaja Mosque–Bibi Raje.

23-012.r: Kirti Stambha Prashasti → composed by Atri Kavi (with Mahesh); tower built by Rana Kumbha after victory over Malwa, under supervision of Jaita.

23-013.r: Kirti Stambha, Chittor → Rana Kumbha, to mark his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa.

23-014.r: Wrong pair: Ajmer–Quwwat-ul-Islam; it is in Delhi. Correct: Jaunpur–Atala Masjid; Malwa–Jahaz Mahal; Gulbarga–Jama Masjid.

23-015.r: 'Lotus bud' fringe under arch → Khaljis; octagonal tomb → Tughluqs; Bodegoi in pillars → Vijayanagara; massive gate with inclined walls → Sharqis.

24-001.r: Kitab-ul-Hind → Al-Biruni (real name Abu Rehan); studied India as a scientist: religion, literature, social and political life.

24-002.r: Tahqiq-i-Hind → Al-Biruni (10-11th century scholar); detailed account of India's history, geography and culture.
24-002.t: Don't confuse with Abdur Razzaq (Vijayanagara) or Barani (Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi).

24-003.r: Amir Khusrau → born 1253 A.D. at Patiyali, Etah district (now Kasganj); 'Tuti-i-Hind' (Parrot of India); first historical Masnavi Qiran-us-Sadain.

24-006.r: Amir Khusrau → pioneer of Khari Boli; loved Hindavi; called himself a 'Turkish-Indian'.

24-007.r: Both Amir Khusrau and Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya saw the reigns of more than seven Delhi Sultans.
24-007.c: No answer printed; the book says both (a) and (b) fit.

24-008.r: Amir Khusrau served many Delhi rulers: Balban, Kaiqubad, Jalaluddin and Alauddin Khalji, Mubarak Shah, Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad-bin-Tughluq; disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.

24-012.r: Amir Khusrau → poet, historian and musician (all); 'Tuti-i-Hind'; promoter of Khari Boli Hindi.

24-013.r: Father of the Persian 'Sabak-i-Hindi' (Hindustani style) → Amir Khusrau; said Hindi words are no less than Persian.

24-014.r: Father of Hindi Khari Boli → Amir Khusrau; promoter of the 'Sabak-i-Hindi' poetic style.

24-015.r: Scholar of both Hindi (Hindavi) and Persian → Amir Khusrau.

24-016.r: First Persian poet to depict the Indian environment in poetry → Amir Khusrau, who served at the courts of more than seven Delhi Sultans.

24-017.r: Amir Khusrau wrote all four: Khazain-ul-Futuh, Nuh Sipihr, Miftah-ul-Futuh, Qiran-us-Sadain.

24-018.r: Both correct: Kitab-i-Nauras (songs on Hindu deities and Muslim saints) → Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur (capital Nauraspur); Amir Khusrau began early Qawwali.

24-019.r: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri → Minhaj-us-Siraj, dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud; 23 volumes; English by H.G. Raverty; covers Ghori's conquest.

24-020.r: Order: Kitab-ul-Hind (Al-Biruni) → Prithviraja Raso (Chand Bardai) → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (Minhaj-i-Siraj) → Fatawa-i-Jahandari (Barani).

24-021.r: Ziauddin Barani → Fatwa-i-Jahandari (political ideals for Muslim rulers) and Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi (history of the Sultanate).

24-022.r: Earliest account of Bakhtiyar Khalji's invasion of Bihar → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-us-Siraj; records Nalanda's sack (1193).

24-023.r: Language patronised by Delhi Sultans → Persian, made the official language after the Sultanate's founding.

24-024.r: 'Apabhramsa' in medieval Sanskrit texts → early forms of modern Indian languages; Hindi dialects, Punjabi, Sindhi, Marathi etc. grew from it.

24-025.r: Barani → Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi; Hasan Nizami → Taj-ul-Maasir; Minhaj-us-Siraj → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Yahia-bin-Ahmad → Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi.

24-026.r: Mirat-e-Sikandari → Gujarat; Burhan-e-Masir → Bahmanis of Ahmadnagar; Riyaz-us-Salatin → Bengal; Riyaz-ul-Insha → Mahmud Gawan's letters.

24-027.r: Futuh-us-Salatin → Isami; Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi → Firuz Shah Tughlaq; Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi → Barani; Khazain-ul-Futuh → Amir Khusrau.

24-028.r: Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi (on Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reign) → Shams Siraj Afif; Ziauddin Barani also wrote a Tughlaq history of the same name.

24-029.r: Taj-ul-Maasir → Hasan Nizami; Khazain-ul-Futuh → Amir Khusrau; Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi → Yahia bin Ahmad Sarhindi; Fatwa-i-Jahandari → Barani.

24-031.r: 'Tarikh-i-Firozshahi' → two different books by Ziauddin Barani and Shams-i-Siraj Afif, same title, different content.

24-032.r: Tarikh-i-Hind → Al-Biruni; Tarikh-i-Delhi → Khusrau; Rihla → Ibn Battuta; Tabaqat-i-Nasiri → Minhaj-us-Siraj.

24-033.r: Haqaiq-i-Hindi → Abdul Wahid Bilgrami; Tahdhibul Akhlaq → Ibn Miskawayh; Kunzal Tijar → Bailaq al-Qabayaki; Jawamiul Hikayat → Sadruddin Muhammad 'Aufi'.

24-034.r: Fawaid-ul-Fuad (Nizamuddin Auliya's conversations) → compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi.
24-034.t: Not Amir Khusrau, though both were Nizamuddin's disciples.

24-035.r: Finest Hindu-Muslim harmony in instruments → Sitar; credited to Amir Khusrau, mixing the Iranian Tambura and Indian Veena; he added melodies Iman, Zilf, Sajgari.

24-036.r: Tabla (and Sitar) → credited to Amir Khusrau (13th/14th century); first author to use Hindavi words.

24-037.r: Tutinama (Persian version of Chintamani Bhatt's Suka Saptati) → Khwaja Ziya-uddin Nakhshabi, 14th-century physician and Sufi of Badayun.

24-038.r: Rajput ruler who wrote on music → Rana Kumbha (Sangeet Raj, also called Sangeet Mimansa); built Kirti Stambha after beating Mahmud Khalji (1440-1448 AD).

24-039.r: Correct pair: Pundrik Vitthal–Raagmala. Bhavbhatta → Anup Sangeet Ratnakar; Kumbha → Sangitraja; Chand Khan → Delhi gharana of khayal.

24-040.r: Ragamala → Pundrik Vitthal; Rasa Kaumudi → Sri Kantha; Raga Vibodh → Somanath; Chaturdandi Prakashika → Venkatamakhin.
24-040.c: No answer printed; question names Venkatraman instead of Venkatamakhin; otherwise code (a) 3 4 1 2 fits.

24-041.r: Ras Panchadhyayi → Nand Das (Braj); Chaitanya Bhagavata → Vrindavan Das (Bengali); Chaitanya Mangal → Jayananda; Bhakti Ratnakara → Narahari Chakravarti.

24-042.r: Delhi Sultan who wrote his memoirs → Firuz Tughluq, 'Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi', to present himself as an ideal Muslim ruler.

24-043.r: Mirat-e-Sikandari: both true; describes the prosperity of Sultan Mahmud Begada's Gujarat and the safety of trade routes for merchants.
